props.title: King Kong Lives

sections.content: **King Kong Lives** (1986) represents one of cinema's most misguided monster movie sequels, arriving a decade after the 1976 **King Kong** remake. The film's premise - Kong surviving his fall from the World Trade Center and receiving an artificial heart transplant - demonstrates how far the mighty ape had fallen from his groundbreaking 1933 debut. Director John Guillermin returned from the '76 version, but lightning didn't strike twice. The film's attempt to create a "romance" between Kong and a female giant ape named Lady Kong feels more like a B-movie parody than a serious entry in the Kong franchise.

sections.content: The failure of **King Kong Lives** (1986) highlights how the Kong character works best when treated with gravity and wonder, as Peter Jackson would later demonstrate with **King Kong** (2005). The '86 sequel's bargain-basement effects and soap opera plotting stand in stark contrast to the original's groundbreaking technical achievements. While **Son of Kong** (1933) had already proven that Kong sequels were tricky territory, at least that film maintained some of the original's charm and practical effects mastery. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Movie Monsters

The 1980s saw many classic movie monsters stumble into questionable territory. While **Aliens** (1986) successfully reinvented its creature, films like **Jaws: The Revenge** (1987) and **King Kong Lives** (1986) demonstrated how franchises could go terribly wrong. The decade's emphasis on practical effects and animatronics should have given Kong an advantage, but the film's execution falls far below contemporary monster features like **The Thing** (1982) or **An American Werewolf in London** (1981).
